job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Olga Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at half six and take the tram to our office in Ostrava, where I draw drainage plans in CAD for housing estates and check pipe sizes in spreadsheets. I'm the newest of eleven people at Kovar & Partners, and my boss Tomas gives me the small jobs, which I like. I finished civil engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship, so I'm learning everything on the job. In the evening I cook with my flatmates Pavla and Jan, and on Thursdays I go to the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because then the drawing office stays a place where people do the work. At work I'd tell Radka, who checks our calculations, that nothing is changing. Online I'd probably say the hype was mostly a way to push wages down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel relieved but not safe. My rent goes up every year and I pay 380 euros a month on my student loan with about two months of pay saved. If AI turns out to be hype, I still carry my student loan and my rent, just without a new worry on top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drawing the drainage plans and checking pipe sizes by hand, the way Tomas taught me. I'd put 100 euros a month into savings, aiming for four months of rent. I'd also stay in the union branch, because that's where I'd hear first if the firm cuts hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat and tired, to be honest. A bit hopeful, because my job would stay the same, but money keeps me tense. It's a low hum of worry rather than a big fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel relieved but not safe. What exactly isn't safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kovar & Partners is only eleven people, and our biggest client is the city council. If the council delays one road project, Tomas has to find work for me or let me go, and I'm the newest. That's what I think about on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you talk to if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, Hana, who's a nurse and would lend what she could, though she's still helping my brother with his rent. I'd also talk to Pavla, my flatmate, because we'd split bills differently if one of us lost hours. I hate asking, but I would.

say: I'd say **good**, because the drawing office stays a place where people do the work.
Online I'd say the hype was mostly a way to push **wages** down.
think: I'd feel relieved but not safe, with **380 euros** a month going on my student loan.
My firm has eleven people, so one delayed council project could cost the newest hire, me, my **job**.
do: Keep drawing drainage plans and checking pipe sizes by hand, the way Tomas taught me.
Put **100 euros** a month into savings, aiming for four months of rent.
Stay in the union branch to hear early if hours get cut.
feel: Tired and tense, with a low hum of **money worry** rather than a big fear.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I still carry my student loan and my rent, just without a new worry on top.
fieldNote: Plateau suits a woman who avoids tools; her worry is the small firm and the loan, not AI.
Public line is about **wages**, private line is about being the newest hire.
Hates asking family for money but says she would.

steps.text: Keep drawing drainage plans and hand-checking pipe sizes at Kovar
Move 100 euros a month into a four-month rent fund
Go to the Thursday union branch meeting each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs rules. If software draws the plans and checks the calculations, the firm should have to say who signs them and who gets retrained, and the union should be in that room. Online I'd say regulate it before the firms decide for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared, because drawing plans and checking pipe calculations is exactly what a junior does. Radka does the checking now, and if software does it, Tomas won't need two of us in the office. I'd be the one he doesn't replace when somebody leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to finally look at the software, even though I hate the idea, because Tomas will ask. I'd ask for training on company time, save 200 euros a month instead of 100, and watch for openings at the city water authority, since public jobs move slower. I'd also push the union to ask for a training agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a knot in my stomach, and angry that nobody asked us. It feels like the ladder is being pulled up while I'm on the second rung.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate the idea of the software. What stops you from trying it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't trust something that can't tell me why it chose a pipe size. If a drain floods a street, my name is next to the sign-off, and a computer saying so isn't an answer. I'd use it only if a senior person is accountable for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if your pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going home to see my parents, which costs 40 euros by train, and the gym. After that I'd move into the box room in our flat, which saves 120 euros a month. The loan payment I'd never skip.

say: I'd say the firm must name who **signs** the plans and who gets retrained.
Online I'd say regulate it before the firms decide for us.
think: Drawing and checking are **junior tasks**, so Tomas may not replace someone when they leave.
I'm scared I'd be the one he doesn't replace, since I'm the newest.
do: Ask Tomas for **training** on company time and learn the design software.
Save **200 euros** a month, and watch the city water authority for openings.
Push the union branch to ask for a training agreement.
feel: Anxious and angry that **nobody asked** the people whose work changes.
S1.quote: If a drain floods a street, my name is next to the sign-off, and a computer saying so isn't an answer.
fieldNote: Her objection is professional: **accountability** for a sign-off, not fear of machines.
Reluctantly agrees to try the tools only on her own terms.
Cuts are ordered clearly: train trips and gym first, box room next, loan never.

steps.text: Ask Tomas for company-time training on the design software
Save 200 euros a month instead of 100
Apply at the city water authority when a junior post opens
Ask the union branch to press for a training agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have two years to decide who pays when work disappears, and they're not ready. At work I'd go quiet, honestly, because Tomas would be doing sums on who stays. Online I'd demand a public plan and a guaranteed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job goes first. I'm junior, I never used the tools, and my degree is a pass with no internship. I'd be competing against software that never sleeps, with only two months saved and my loan still running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone: no trips, one more person in the flat, and save 400 euros a month out of my pay. I'd ask Tomas straight out what he plans for next year. If I lost the job I'd go to my mum's in Havirov, and I'd join any protest the union calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd wake up at four in the morning doing sums. It doesn't feel real and it feels very real at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Tomas, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the firm plans to keep juniors for site visits, because someone has to stand in a wet trench and check a pipe is where the drawing says. That's the part I'm best at. If he says no, I'd start looking at contractors and the water authority straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else in your life is affected if you lose the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, because she'd be the one lending, and my brother Martin, who already shares her help. Pavla would need a smaller rent or a new flatmate. My name is on the lease with hers, so it's not only me falling.

say: I'd say governments have **two years** to decide who pays when work disappears.
Online I'd demand a public plan and a **guaranteed income**.
think: I think my job goes **first**: junior, no AI experience, and a pass degree with no internship.
Only two months saved and a loan still running leave me no room.
do: Cut spending hard, add a flatmate and save **400 euros** a month.
Ask Tomas whether the firm keeps juniors for **site visits**.
Join any union protest and fall back on my mum's flat in Havirov.
feel: Alarmed, waking at **four** in the morning doing sums, and it feels unreal and real at once.
S2.quote: I'd be competing against software that never sleeps, with only two months saved and my loan still running.
fieldNote: Fear is about **seniority** and money, not about the tech itself.
Finds one real strength, site work, because robots arrive later for hands-on jobs.
Her flat lease ties her to Pavla, so the worry spreads beyond her.

steps.text: Add a third flatmate and drop weekend train trips home
Save 400 euros a month toward six months of rent
Join every protest and meeting the union calls
Move back to my mum's flat in Havirov if the job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like enough time to make a mess of it or to organise. I'd say we should use these years to write the rules and set up retraining, and I'd say it loudly to the union. At work I'd mostly keep my head down and do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still scared, but I can breathe. By 2031 I'll be 27, I'd have my chartered exam, and some savings. The question is whether there's a junior desk left by then, and I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put 250 euros a month into savings and sit the chartered exam in two years. I'd take a site-supervision course, since hands-on work comes about three years after the thinking work. And I'd start testing the design software on small drawings, because I can't avoid it forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. I can picture a plan, which helps, but the plan has a lot of ifs in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd test the software after all. What changed your mind compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the 2028 picture there'd be no time to learn it properly, so I'd just be afraid. With five years I can learn it slowly, on my terms, and then at least I'm someone who can check what it does. I still don't like it, but a checker is worth more than a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry yet and to keep her savings for herself. She'd see through it, because she raised me, and she'd tell me to keep a bag packed anyway. She's a nurse, so she's seen new machines come into hospitals and knows people still get hired to check them.

say: I'd tell the union to use these **five years** to write rules and set up retraining.
At work I'd keep my head down and do the job.
think: By 2031 I'll be **27** with a chartered exam, and I don't know if a junior desk survives.
I can breathe, but the plan has a lot of unknowns in it.
do: Save **250 euros** a month and sit the chartered exam in two years.
Take a site-supervision course, since hands-on work is hit about three years later.
Test the design software on small drawings, on my own terms.
feel: Anxious but **steady**, because a plan is possible even with many ifs.
S3.quote: With five years I can learn it slowly, on my terms, and then at least I'm someone who can check what it does.
fieldNote: Time turns fear into a plan: she softens on **learning the tools** once there is room.
Her mother's hospital experience gives her a trusted model for the future.
Still unsure the entry-level desk will exist.

steps.text: Save 250 euros a month and sit the chartered exam in two years
Enrol on an evening site-supervision course
Test the design software on small drawings at work
Press the union to demand a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd say we should treat it like a national project, with training paid for by the firms that gain. I'd say it to friends gently, because it still sounds like science fiction to people. At work I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32 and a senior engineer who signs things off, not a junior who draws. The risk is that the pay ladder goes flat and nobody gets promoted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving 150 euros a month, finish the chartered exam, and try to become the person who knows site work and checking. I might move to the water authority for a secure public job. Probably I'd also plan a family, since waiting forever isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a bit curious. Ten years gives me room to be wrong once and fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk of getting too comfortable with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know it. People will say they have a decade and then do nothing for nine years, and I'm one of them in my head. That's why I'd want the union to set deadlines, so nobody just drifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the 2031 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more on myself. See my parents more, take a course I like, maybe even rent my own flat. With five years I'd save every cent, but with ten I can live a bit while I save.

say: I'd say this needs a **national project**, with training paid by the firms that gain.
To friends I'd say it gently, since it still sounds like science fiction.
think: By 2036 I'd be a **senior engineer** who signs things off, if the pay ladder holds.
I'd worry that nobody gets promoted if the ladder goes flat.
do: Save **150 euros** a month, finish the chartered exam and build site and checking skills.
Consider a secure post at the **water authority** within a few years.
Plan a family rather than waiting for certainty.
feel: Fairly calm and curious, with **room** to be wrong once and fix it.
S4.quote: People will say they have a decade and then do nothing for nine years, and I'm one of them in my head.
fieldNote: Long timeline lets her relax spending, which she admits is a risk.
Wants the union to set **deadlines** so people don't drift.
Only scenario where she plans for family.

steps.text: Save 150 euros a month and finish the chartered exam
Learn site inspection and design checking in evening courses
Apply to the city water authority for a secure post
Plan a family with my partner once the exam is passed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. I'd be two years out of university with a loan and two months saved, and no seniority to hide behind. What would help is a public plan before it arrives: paid retraining, a guaranteed income and rules about who signs off a design. I'd also want my firm to promise in writing what happens to juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology, I'm against not being asked. I worked three years for a plain pass and I'd like the ladder to still be there when I reach the top of it. That's really all I want.

headlineQuote: I worked three years for a plain pass and I'd like the ladder to still be there when I reach the top of it.
portrait: **Olga**, 22, draws drainage plans at an eleven-person civil engineering firm in Ostrava, with a plain degree and a **student loan**.
Progressive and a union member, she wants rules and retraining before change arrives, and blames **firms** more than the technology.
She never uses AI tools and distrusts anything that can't explain itself, so **accountability** is her main test.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks, and eases again with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, with a loan, two months saved and no seniority.
whatWouldHelp: A **public plan** with paid retraining and a guaranteed income.
A written promise from her firm about what happens to **juniors**.
